uncited: Application-Specific Extensions modify the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework to handle non-RGB, non-photometric data or to extract explicit geometry from the implicit volumetric representation [1875-volumetric-gaussian-splatting-avis.md], [3301-gaussian-splatting-for-microscopy.md], [5170-ultragauss-rendering.md], [8498-surface-and-mesh-extraction.md].

While standard 3DGS optimizes for novel-view synthesis of RGB scenes using calibrated camera poses and photometric losses, these adaptations replace the projection target with volumetric supervision, voxel-space rasterization, or 3D geometric intersections [1875-volumetric-gaussian-splatting-avis.md], [3301-gaussian-splatting-for-microscopy.md], [5170-ultragauss-rendering.md].

All extensions in this family retain the core 3DGS primitive representation: a set of $M$ anisotropic 3D Gaussian kernels $\mathcal{G} = \{G_i\}_{i=1}^M$ [Radiative Gaussian Splatting](3040-radiative-gaussian-splatting.md), [1875-volumetric-gaussian-splatting-avis.md].
However, the attribute representation and loss functions diverge significantly from the standard RGB opacity/color model.

In radiative and domain-specific variants, this is replaced by view-independent scalar attributes or feature vectors [Radiative Gaussian Splatting](3040-radiative-gaussian-splatting.md), [1875-volumetric-gaussian-splatting-avis.md].
3D Gaussian Splatting was originally introduced for real-time novel-view synthesis of RGB scenes [1795-3d-gaussian-splatting.md].
The extension to application-specific domains emerged as researchers sought to leverage the differentiable nature and fast rendering of Gaussians for scientific imaging and geometric analysis.
Radiative variants were developed to align the splatting model with X-ray physics [Radiative Gaussian Splatting](3040-radiative-gaussian-splatting.md).

Domain-specific adaptations were created to handle medical and microscopy data where volumetric supervision is more appropriate than photometric error [1875-volumetric-gaussian-splatting-avis.md], [3301-gaussian-splatting-for-microscopy.md].
Surface extraction methods address the inherent lack of explicit topology in the Gaussian representation [8498-surface-and-mesh-extraction.md].
